name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,303

entries.clue: Psychiatrist’s contract (6)

blocks.note: slang from 'headshrinker', a joking name for a psychiatrist
the verb: to get smaller, not a legal document

annotation.surface: A psychiatrist's employment contract.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining the two meanings. 'Contract' looks like a noun, a legal document, but it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang for a psychiatrist comes from 'headshrinker'; as a verb it is a plain synonym for contract, to get smaller.

entries.clue: Large crowd he’s taken round old road (5)

indicators.note: HE is wrapped round the other letters, holding them inside

blocks.note: taken as written; the outer letters
O is the standard abbreviation for old
RD is the abbreviation for road

annotation.surface: A man who has led a large crowd along an old road.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s is short for 'has': he has taken round, so the pronoun splits to go either side of the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a horde is a large, often unruly, crowd.

entries.clue: Giving full details of home department hotel (2,5)

blocks.note: at home = in
DEPT is the abbreviation for department
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A report detailing the Home Department's hotel bill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home department' reads as one government office, like the Home Office (the UK ministry for domestic affairs), but it splits in two.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: an account done in depth covers the subject thoroughly, leaving no detail out.

entries.clue: Sportswear set for assembly (3)

blocks.note: British word for a team's playing strip
a box of parts to be put together, as for a model

annotation.surface: Sports clothing laid out ready for a school assembly.
annotation.walkthrough: In British usage a sports team's uniform is its kit; 'assembly' is not a school gathering but putting parts together.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the clothing and equipment for a sport, and a packaged set of parts to build something.

entries.clue: Site contains a magnificent residence (6)

indicators.note: the site 'contains' the next word in its literal sense of holding it inside, so A goes within PLACE

blocks.note: a site is a place
taken as written

annotation.surface: A building site that includes a grand house.
annotation.walkthrough: The single letter goes in straight after the first letter of the site.
annotation.definitionFit: A palace is the official home of a monarch or bishop, the model of a grand residence.

entries.clue: Act almost had to go through (9)

indicators.note: the word is not quite complete: its last letter goes

blocks.note: act = PERFORM, minus its last letter
had (a meal) = ate

annotation.surface: A law that was nearly obliged to be passed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like legislation, and 'go through' like a bill passing; in fact act means perform and go through means pierce.
annotation.definitionFit: To perforate is to pierce with holes, so to go right through a surface.

entries.clue: Clear openings for lawbreakers upset detectives (5)

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letters of lawbreakers and upset
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

annotation.surface: Obvious chances for criminals have annoyed the detectives.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like a reversal instruction but is just one of the two words supplying first letters. CID is the plain-clothes branch of British police.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lucid writing or thinking is clear and easy to follow.

entries.clue: Brave guy in bed for a smoke (7)

indicators.note: a brave guy 'in bed' is lying inside it, so HERO is placed within COT

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
a hero is a brave man

annotation.surface: A bold man lying in bed with a cigarette.
annotation.walkthrough: The brave guy goes after the first letter of the bed, not at its start.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar with both ends cut square, so 'a smoke' in the everyday sense of something smoked.

entries.clue: Extremely clever reviser of text, to whom I’m indebted (8)

indicators.note: take the extremes, the two end letters

blocks.note: the end letters of clever
an editor revises text

annotation.surface: Praise for a brilliant editor to whom the writer owes a debt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely clever' reads as high praise, but extremely asks for the outer letters. The definition is a descriptive phrase for the person owed money.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the creditor is the person a debt is owed to, seen from the debtor's side.

entries.clue: Prepare to swallow cold cut (4)

blocks.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
to hew is to cut, as with an axe

annotation.surface: Getting ready to eat a slice of cold meat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold cut' reads as a slice of meat; it splits into two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: chewing breaks food down so it can be swallowed.

entries.clue: Turn on waterworks with very little pressure (4)

blocks.note: wee is Scottish for small
P is the symbol for pressure

annotation.surface: Opening the water mains when the pressure is very low.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn on the waterworks' is an idiom for starting to cry, dressed up here as a plumbing job.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to turn on the waterworks is to start crying, often for effect.

entries.clue: Little flower in cold fall (8)

blocks.note: a small white bulb that flowers in late winter
read literally: a fall of the cold white stuff

annotation.surface: A small flower seen during a cold autumn.
annotation.walkthrough: The second meaning is playful: 'fall' reads as autumn, but a fall of snow is a snow drop, split into its two parts.
annotation.definitionFit: The snowdrop is a small white flower of late winter; the second sense is cryptic, a literal drop of snow.

entries.clue: Perhaps Oscar Wilde caught at last, breaking law (9)

indicators.note: take the last letter of each word
ET breaks into STATUTE, splitting it

blocks.note: a statute is a law
the last letters of Wilde and caught

annotation.surface: Oscar Wilde, finally arrested for breaking the law.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar Wilde really was jailed, which makes the surface convincing; the name splits, Oscar joining 'Perhaps' as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an Oscar, the Academy Award, is one kind of statuette, which 'Perhaps' signals.

entries.clue: A maths broadcast is source of inspiring problems (6)

indicators.note: letters scattered, as seed is broadcast

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: A televised maths lesson that sets students puzzling problems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' is used literally: breathing in. 'Maths' is the British word for math.
annotation.definitionFit: Asthma causes difficulty breathing in, problems with inspiring in its literal sense.

entries.clue: Mobility device firm put in store for renovation (7)

indicators.note: CO is inserted into the other letters
STORE is renovated, its letters rearranged

blocks.note: STORE rearranged
CO is the abbreviation for company

annotation.surface: A company brings a mobility scooter into a shop being refitted.
annotation.walkthrough: The firm sits after the first letter of the rearranged shop.
annotation.definitionFit: A mobility scooter is a small motorised vehicle for people who have trouble walking.

entries.clue: Divides up bulbs for cooking (not the first two) (6)

blocks.note: shallots are small onions
SH removed

annotation.surface: Splitting onions for a recipe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bulbs' suggests flowers or light bulbs; 'for cooking' pins it to the onion family.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to allot is to share out portions, dividing something up among people.

entries.clue: Caught one without protective coat (7)

indicators.note: caught as in heard, caught what someone said

blocks.note: one who lacks, one without

annotation.surface: Someone arrested without a coat on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like C, the cricket abbreviation, but it means heard. The one without is a made-up word, a person who lacks.
annotation.definitionFit: Lacquer is a hard varnish brushed on to seal and protect a surface.

entries.clue: Messy room used for lengthy sleeper (8)

indicators.note: the letters are in a mess, jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: An untidy bedroom where someone sleeps for hours.
annotation.walkthrough: The sleeper is an animal, not a person or a railway carriage.
annotation.definitionFit: The dormouse hibernates for months, and is proverbially sleepy, as at the Mad Hatter's tea party.

entries.clue: Person in charge is frantically busy (5)

blocks.note: a man is a person
IC = in charge, as in 2IC, second in command

annotation.surface: The boss is run off their feet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Person in charge' looks like one phrase for a boss; it is two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a manic day or person is wildly, frantically active.

entries.clue: Cloak and headgear, last of range (4)

indicators.note: the 'last of' a word is the letter that ends it, so only the final letter of range is used

blocks.note: a cap is headgear
the final letter of range

annotation.surface: The final items in a clothing range: a cloak and a hat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cloak and headgear' reads as a list of clothes; only cloak is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cape is a short sleeveless cloak.

entries.clue: Iron the newspapers (5)

blocks.note: the verb: to smooth clothes with a hot iron
collective name for journalism, from the printing machine

annotation.surface: An instruction to iron out the creases in the papers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Iron' could be the metal, but here it is the household verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: pressing clothes smooths them as ironing does, and the press is the collective name for newspapers.

entries.clue: Heads turned in shock (4)

blocks.note: nut is slang for head

annotation.surface: People turning their heads in surprise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heads turned' reads as people looking around; nut is slang for head, as in 'use your nut'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a blow or piece of news can stun, leaving someone dazed with shock.

entries.clue: Partly shaved heads of thugs on news somehow upset residents every day (8)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: thugs on news somehow upset residents every day
blocks.note: first letters of eight words

annotation.surface: Skinhead thugs in the news are upsetting the locals daily.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal, but every word after 'heads of' just supplies its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Tonsure is the monk's shaved crown with a ring of hair left around it, so the head is only partly shaved.

entries.clue: Small bite and small drink (3)

blocks.note: a little pinch with the teeth
a small measure of spirits

annotation.surface: A snack and a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Both meanings are nouns; the clue's appeal is how ordinary it looks.
annotation.definitionFit: Two noun senses of one word: a quick pinching bite, and a small measure of spirits.

entries.clue: Old, unusually clear prophecy (6)

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in an unusual way

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
CLEAR rearranged

annotation.surface: An ancient prediction that was, for once, unambiguous.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke about oracles, famous for riddling answers.
annotation.definitionFit: The word can mean the prophetic pronouncement itself, not only the one who makes it.

entries.clue: Study American country’s energy (6)

blocks.note: a country in South America
the possessive S, taken as written
E is the symbol for energy

annotation.surface: Researching a nation's energy policy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American' suggests the USA, but the country is in South America.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to read through carefully, to study in detail.
